Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette: Kwame had been nineteen when the stalking began, a quiet escalation that eventually turned his routines into a series of monitored paths. It started during his senior year, when a woman he had met at a campus tech fair began appearing in his periphery. He had given her his email, smiled when they crossed paths, and answered her messages promptly. What frightened him most was the sudden realization that his own responsiveness had opened a door he could not close. Within weeks, she began leaving unrequested packages at his apartment door, tagging him in social media posts, and following his commute. The breaking point came on a rain-slicked Tuesday in October: he turned a corner outside his building and found her waiting under the awning, her eyes fixed on him, her phone already recording. He was certain that his casual wave and his habit of checking his screen had signaled permission for her to stay close. From that day forward, Kwame had come to believe the world was a dangerous place, where ordinary proximity could quickly become surveillance. He found himself constantly scanning the street for familiar silhouettes, glancing at phone screens the moment they lit up, and rehearsing his routes before stepping out the door. The vigilance settled into his shoulders, a quiet hum that never quite faded. He was convinced, too, that he bore responsibility for the intrusion, tracing the escalation to his own actions: his tendency to reply quickly, his habit of sharing location tags, his casual eye contact that he now read as an invitation. Each new notification felt like a thread pulling him back into that October tension, and he would pause, thumb hovering, wondering if he had done something to warrant the attention. His PCL-5 score of 65 captured the steady weight of these perceptions, which co-existed in his daily life without demanding that one explain the other. His transition to a junior UX Designer role coincided with the deepening of these patterns. In the glass-walled design studio, where live user-analytics dashboards streamed across dual monitors and digital notifications pinged in rapid succession, Kwame's monitoring became operational. He avoided checking the messaging tab during design reviews, fearing a familiar name or an unexpected tag would fracture his focus. He began routing his afternoon walks away from the main lobby, where the building's security cameras and the street's foot traffic merged into a single, watchful gaze. Over the following months, these habits accumulated. He stopped answering calls after six, kept his apartment blinds drawn until late afternoon, and declined social invitations that required leaving the house during peak hours. At work, his careful navigation of the open-plan office meant he missed casual team lunches, and his deliberate, measured responses to client emails made his teammates wonder if he was disengaged. His apartment, once a refuge, felt like a staging ground for potential incursions, and he found himself locking and unlocking the deadbolt in quiet, repeated sequences. The tipping point arrived on a Thursday evening when a design prototype he was testing triggered a cascade of cross-app notifications. As his phone chimed in rapid succession, the overlapping sounds mirrored the October rain and the stalker's approach, and he realized he could no longer predict what would appear next. He had come to believe that if he stopped watching, something would slip past unnoticed, and the world would close in once more. What he hoped for now was a way to trust his own boundaries without bracing for impact. He was seeking help because the constant checking had begun to blur his days, and he wanted to understand how to step through his front door again without rehearsing his movements.
